To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
with experience, visually evoked oscillation prevalence in primary visual cortex (area V1) relates to the expected time to future reward and to the rate at which reward is experienced.
with training, cue-evoked activity in visual cortex evolves to convey expected reward rate and expected reward time.

(1) repeated presentation of visual stimuli evokes theta band (4–10 Hz) oscillatory activity in V1, and (2) with training, this theta band activity relates to the expected timing of future reward and to experienced reward rate, and (3) these changes occur in the absence of any change in the physical properties of the stimulus.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how experience induces the emergence of oscillatory activity in visual cortex and how this activity relates to the animal's experience.
understanding how visual cortex activity reflects the significance of visual stimuli, not just their physical properties, and how experience can alter this relationship.
how visual cortical oscillations emerge with experience to convey expected reward and experienced reward rate.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the visual cortex does not only represent physical features of the stimuli but also their behavioral significance.
the emergence of visually induced oscillations is a form of perceptual learning.
the oscillatory activity in V1 reflects the expected reward time and reward rate, which is an important aspect of learning and decision making.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual cortex can learn to convey the expected reward time and experienced reward rate of the animal.

the visual system is not only a faithful conveyor of visual information, it is also a dynamic system that adapts to the behavioral significance of visual stimuli, and in the process, conveys information that is relevant for guiding behavior.
the visual system is more flexible than previously thought, and that the emergence of theta oscillations in V1 is not simply the result of perceptual learning, but also the result of reward learning.
The main takeaway from our work is that
experience-dependent changes in visual cortex are not always about improving visual perception.
experience-dependent changes in visual cortical oscillations are not limited to improving visual perception.
V1 is not a passive conduit of visual information but rather a dynamic system that is shaped by experience to encode the significance of visual stimuli.
